title: Gun dog
wiki_lead:
Gun dogs (gundogs) or bird dogs  are types of hunting dogs developed to assist hunters in finding and retrieving game, typically various fowls that are shot down on the wing (in flight). The term hunting dog is broad and includes all breeds and skills of hunting canines, but "gun dogs" refers to canines that are trained to work alongside a loud firearm while hunting or retrieving game.
Gun dogs are categorized by their usage. Due to the range of capabilities of different breeds of gun dogs, different breeds may fall under the definitions of multiple categories. The United Kennel Club divides gun dogs into four non-exclusive categories: retrievers, pointers, setters, and flushing spaniels.
While The United Kennel Club describes the fourth category of gun dogs to be flushing spaniels, there are other non-spaniel types of dogs which can be used for flushing.

Types
There are several breeds used as gundogs with varying instinctive skill sets for each one. 


List of gundog breeds


History
In the seventeenth century, the French practice of shooting birds in flight was brought to England and Wales by King Charles II. Various spaniels and setters were used as gun dogs for this activity until the pointer was introduced from Spain in the early eighteenth century. In time, more breeds would be used as gun dogs, each with their own characteristics, and the term “gundog" would be coined by the late eighteenth century. The adoption of the breech-loading shotgun in the nineteenth century improved efficiency in hunting and the demand for well trained gun dogs increased. This increased demand led to the organization of dog shows and kennel clubs.


Kennel club classification
When competing in conformation shows most kennel clubs, including The Kennel Club, group pedigree gun dog breeds together in their own gun dog group, whilst some such as the American Kennel Club group them in a sporting group. The term "sporting" more accurately reflects historical hunting and fishing styles for which many pointers, setters, flushing spaniels, water dogs, retrievers and decoy dogs were developed to work in conjunction with nets, traps, hawks, sighthounds, arrows and bolts rather than firearms.
grok_lead: A gun dog, also known as a sporting dog, is a type of hunting dog bred and trained to assist hunters in the field by locating, flushing, pointing at, or retrieving game, particularly in conjunction with the use of firearms. These dogs are prized for their natural instincts, such as a keen sense of smell, endurance, and often water-repellent coats that enable them to work in diverse terrains including wetlands and uplands. The development of gun dogs traces back to the 17th and 18th centuries in Europe, particularly in Britain and continental countries, when the widespread adoption of shoulder-fired guns necessitated dogs that could adapt to shooting from a distance rather than close-range pursuit. Prior to this, hunting relied more on falcons, bows, or packs of hounds, but the gun dog's role emerged as sportsmen selectively bred versatile companions from existing spaniel, hound, and water dog lineages to handle shot game without damaging it. By the 19th century, organized breeding programs in England and Germany refined these traits, leading to the recognition of distinct breeds by kennel clubs. Gun dogs are typically classified into three main types based on their specialized functions: pointing breeds (such as pointers and setters), which use their stance to indicate the location of game to allow for a clear shot; flushing breeds (such as spaniels), which drive birds from cover toward the hunter; and retrievers, which fetch downed or wounded quarry, often from water. Notable breeds include the English Springer Spaniel for flushing, the Labrador Retriever for water work, the German Shorthaired Pointer for versatile pointing, and the Irish Setter for elegant field performance. These dogs require rigorous training to respond to commands, remain steady to gunfire, and exhibit soft mouths for gentle retrieval, making them not only effective hunters but also loyal family companions when properly socialized.
